Supplementary Information
    AMPGen: An Evolutionary Information-Reserved and Diffusion-Driven
      Generative Model for de novo Design of Antimicrobial Peptides
Shuwen Jin, Zihan Zeng, Xiyan Xiong, Baicheng Huang, Li Tang, Hongsheng Wang, Xiao Ma,
Xiaochun Tang, Guoqing Shao, Xingxu Huang, and Feng Lin

Fig. S1 The ROC curves illustrate the performance of the XGBoost-based AMP
classifier model across ten-fold cross-validation. Each curve represents the Receiver
Operating Characteristic (ROC) for one fold, showing the trade-off between the true
positive rate and false positive rate at various threshold settings. The average ROC
curve, indicated by the bold line, summarizes the overall model performance, with the
area under the curve (AUC) as a measure of the classification accuracy.

Fig. S2 Performance of LSTM-based predictive models for AMP activity against
bacterial strains. The scatter plots in panels (a) and (b) illustrate the relationship
between the predicted and true log10-transformed minimum inhibitory concentration
(MIC) values for AMPs against E. coli (a) and S. aureus (b), respectively. Each point
represents an AMP candidate, with predicted values on the y-axis and true values on
the x-axis. The red dashed line indicates the ideal fit where predicted values perfectly
match true values (y = x). The coefficient of determination (R²) is shown in the top left
corner of each panel, with R² = 0.8909 for E. coli and R² = 0.8608 for S. aureus,
demonstrating the high predictive accuracy of the LSTM-based models for both
bacterial strains.

Fig. S3 General features of generated raw peptide sequences.
(a) The proportion of each amino acid in the clean generated sequence of each group

(Seq-based、MSA-based and MSA-conditional) without any screening. Sequences

containing ambiguous amino acids have been removed. (b)-(k) Distribution diagrams
of physicochemical properties of the clean generated sequence. The height of each
curve represents the number of sequences. Hydrophilic amino acid in (k) includes
alanine (Ala), valine (Val), leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), methionine (Met),
phenylalanine (Phe), tryptophan (Trp), troline (Pro) and glycine (Gly).

Fig. S4 Distribution of physicochemical properties of AMP candidates.
Candidate AMP sequences refer to all sequences that have passed the discriminator.
Panels (a), (b), and (c) show the distributions of molecular weight, aliphatic index,
hydropathicity, and proportion of hydrophobic amino acids, respectively, for the MSA-
conditional group (red), compared to the MSA-based (green) and seq-based (blue)
baselines. The gray shading indicates the density distribution, highlighting the
concentration of sequences within specific property ranges. Hydrophobic amino acid in
(d) includes alanine (Ala), valine (Val), leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), methionine
(Met), phenylalanine (Phe), tryptophan (Trp), troline (Pro) and glycine (Gly).

Fig. S5 Violin plots comparing the distribution of physicochemical properties
between the AMP candidates. Panels (a) through (f) illustrate the distribution of
different properties across three generation types: the baseline seq-based (blue),
baseline MSA-based (green), and MSA-conditional (red). Candidate AMP sequences
include all sequences that passed the discriminator. The dividing lines within the violin
plot represent the mean, as well as the upper and lower quartiles. Significant differences
are observed between any two groups in each figure (p < 0.001, Kruskal-Wallis multiple
comparison, with p-values adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method).

Fig. S6. Hemolytic potential of the validated AMPs.
Hemolysis curves of AMP variants (AMP-4, 15, 17, 20, 21, 24, 30, 32, and 35) across
different concentrations. The percentage of hemolysis is plotted against the
concentration of each peptide, ranging from 35 to 1125 μg/mL. The HC50 values,
representing the concentration required to achieve 50% hemolysis, are indicated for
each peptide. Error bars represent the standard deviation (SD) from triplicate
measurements. The lower panels show the visual hemolysis results in erythrocytes for
each corresponding peptide concentration, including controls with Triton X-100
(positive control) and PBS (negative control).

Fig. S7. The cytotoxicity of the validated AMPs.
Cytotoxicity evaluation of AMP variants (AMP-4, 15, 17, 20, 21, 24, 30, 32, and 35)
across different concentrations. The percentage of cell viability related to untreated
control cells is plotted against the concentration of each peptide, ranging from 35 to
1125 μg/mL. The CC50 values, representing the concentration required to achieve 50%
cytotoxicity, are indicated for each peptide. Error bars represent the standard error (SE)
from triplicate measurements.

Fig. S8. Structure of synthetically verified AMPs predicted using PepFold4.
The figure displays the top-ranked structures of 38 synthetically verified AMPs
predicted by PepFold4. The default parameters of PepFold4 were used.

Fig. S9. Distribution of sequence pairwise identity across different studies.
The violin plot shows the distribution of pairwise identity values calculated for
sequences from different models of different studies. Sequence alignment was
performed using the BLOSUM62 matrix applied as the substitution scoring scheme for
comparison. Each group represents a set of AMP sequences designed by a reported
model (‘Study3’ corresponds to the ID 3 model listed in Table S10). The width of the
violin at each value indicates the density of pairwise identities, with wider sections
representing more frequent values. Statistical significance between groups was assessed
using the Kruskal-Wallis test. The global p-value is indicated on the plot.

Fig. S10 Flow diagram of dataset preparation.
The flowchart illustrates the process of constructing datasets for antimicrobial peptide
(AMP) generation and validation. Six primary AMP databases (APD, DADP, DBAASP,
DRAMP, YADAMP, and dbAMP) are used to compile a non-redundant set of 10,249
AMP sequences. This dataset is further used to construct the AMP-MSA dataset, AMP
dataset, and AMP MIC dataset. The AMP-MSA dataset is built by searching UniClust30
with HHblits, consisting of multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) sampled to depth of
16 with a MaxHamming method. The AMP-MSA dataset is utilized by the generator
for AMP sequence design. The AMP dataset, containing 9,964 sequences (5-65 amino
acids in length), is used by the scorer to assess AMP antibacterial potential. The AMP
MIC dataset, including 7,100 sequences targeting Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli) and
6,482 targeting Gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus), was employed by the discriminator
to refine AMP selection. Additionally, the UniProt database is searched to generate the
nonAMP dataset with 11,989 sequences (5-65 amino acids in length), which serves as
a negative dataset by the discriminator and scorer.

Reporting Summary
Nature Portfolio wishes to improve the reproducibility of the work that we publish. This form provides structure for consistency and transparency
in reporting. For further information on Nature Portfolio policies, see our Editorial Policies and the Editorial Policy Checklist.




Statistics
For all statistical analyses, confirm that the following items are present in the figure legend, table legend, main text, or Methods section.
n/a Confirmed
           The exact sample size (n) for each experimental group/condition, given as a discrete number and unit of measurement
           A statement on whether measurements were taken from distinct samples or whether the same sample was measured repeatedly
           The statistical test(s) used AND whether they are one- or two-sided
           Only common tests should be described solely by name; describe more complex techniques in the Methods section.

           A description of all covariates tested
           A description of any assumptions or corrections, such as tests of normality and adjustment for multiple comparisons
           A full description of the statistical parameters including central tendency (e.g. means) or other basic estimates (e.g. regression coefficient)
           AND variation (e.g. standard deviation) or associated estimates of uncertainty (e.g. confidence intervals)

           For null hypothesis testing, the test statistic (e.g. F, t, r) with confidence intervals, effect sizes, degrees of freedom and P value noted
           Give P values as exact values whenever suitable.

           For Bayesian analysis, information on the choice of priors and Markov chain Monte Carlo settings
           For hierarchical and complex designs, identification of the appropriate level for tests and full reporting of outcomes
           Estimates of effect sizes (e.g. Cohen's d, Pearson's r), indicating how they were calculated
                                                Our web collection on statistics for biologists contains articles on many of the points above.



Software and code
Policy information about availability of computer code
  Data collection        The AMP dataset was compiled from six public AMP databases: APD2, DADP, DBAASP（version v3）, DRAMP (version 3.0), YADAMP, and
                         dbAMP (version 2.0). AMP data from these various datasets are merged, deduplicated, and filtered to remove incomplete or meaningless
                         data entries. Finally, our database consisted of 10,249 unique sequences and 9854 items have antibacterial targets of bacteria.
                         The negative dataset (nonAMP sequences) was sourced from the UniProt database. Sequences were filtered to exclude those associated with
                         17 specific keywords: antimicrobial, antibiotic, antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, antimalarial, antiparasitic, anti-protist, anticancer, defense,
                         defensin, cathelicidin, histatin, bacteriocin, microbicidal, fungicide and toxin. As with the positive dataset, sequences containing ambiguous
                         amino acids were excluded, and length was restricted to the range of 5 to 65 amino acids.

  Data analysis          The code used in this study is openly available in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/xiyanxiongnico/AMPGen). This repository includes
                         all scripts and software necessary to replicate the experiments, data analysis, and computational models used in this work. Detailed
                         instructions for installation, usage, and reproduction of the results are also provided in the repository's README file.
                         In addition, we used pre-trained models such as ESM2-t36-3B (https://github.com/facebookresearch/esm), Evodiff-OA_DM_640M and
                         Evodiff-MSA_OA_DM_MAXSUB (https://github.com/microsoft/evodiff).
For manuscripts utilizing custom algorithms or software that are central to the research but not yet described in published literature, software must be made available to editors and
reviewers. We strongly encourage code deposition in a community repository (e.g. GitHub). See the Nature Portfolio guidelines for submitting code & software for further information.
